# Non-Autoregressive and Diffusion Language Models {#sec-nar-lm}

@sec-diffusion described paths through continuous states. Text has categorical
states, and its length is usually not known in advance. Left-to-right decoding
makes each token wait for the one before it. @gls-non-autoregressive generation
shortens that serial dependency by predicting several positions together.
@gls-diffusion adds a forward process that progressively corrupts the data and a
learned reverse process that removes the corruption.
The two ideas overlap, but they are not synonyms. A one-pass translation model
can be non-autoregressive without being a diffusion model, while a block
diffusion model can remain autoregressive across blocks.

The attraction is shorter dependency depth, the number of model evaluations that
must run one after another. For an $L$-token output, @gls-autoregression has $L$
causally ordered decode steps; a masked model, which starts from placeholder
mask tokens and fills them in, may revise all $L$ positions in $K$ rounds. That
does not make its work $L/K$ times cheaper. Each round can score a full
sequence. Every position also attends to positions on both sides, so hidden
states change from round to round. As a result, the usual causal key-value
cache, which stores the attention keys and values already computed for earlier
tokens, cannot be reused unchanged. A useful comparison therefore covers
dependency depth, total model work, output-length handling, and quality under
the same serving setup, in place of a single serial-versus-parallel label.

![Dependency depth under a simple decoding model, on linear axes. Autoregression needs one dependent round per output token, so its line rises with slope one, while an eight-round iterative decoder keeps its round count fixed as length grows. This is algorithmic depth, not measured latency or total compute.](/figures/nar-diffusion-lms-1.svg){#fig-nar-diffusion-lms-1}

## Separate the factorization from the execution plan

Here, $c$ is a source or prompt and $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_L)$ is its output. A
factorization writes the probability of a whole output as a product of simpler
conditional probabilities. An autoregressive model writes

$$
p_\theta(y\mid c)
=\prod_{i=1}^{L}p_\theta(y_i\mid y_{<i},c).
$$

Here, $\theta$ denotes model parameters; $L$ is output length; $y_i$ is token
$i$; and $y_{<i}$ contains the earlier output tokens. The factorization gives a
natural stopping rule because the model can emit an end-of-sequence token. With
a causal @gls-kv-cache, each decode invocation processes one new query position
while reusing keys and values from the prefix.

The original one-shot non-autoregressive translation model instead used

$$
\begin{gathered}
p_\theta(y\mid c,L,z)
=\\[-0.4em]
\prod_{i=1}^{L}p_\theta(y_i\mid c,L,z).
\end{gathered}
$$

where $z$ is an optional latent (unobserved) variable, such as an alignment or
the fertility counts described in the next section. Output
positions share the encoded source and latent variables, but their sampled
tokens do not condition on one another. All positions can therefore be scored
in one model evaluation once $L$ and $z$ are chosen. Across operating points,
Gu et al. reported substantial latency reductions; the smallest reported gap to
the autoregressive teacher whose outputs they trained on was 2 BLEU, while
higher-quality decoding reduced the speed advantage [@gu2017nar]. BLEU
measures n-gram overlap with reference translations. A BLEU difference is
specific to the dataset, tokenization, and decoding setup, so it does not
transfer as a general quality unit.

Iterative models introduce states $y^{(K)},\ldots,y^{(0)}$ and factorize one
refinement step across positions:

$$
\begin{gathered}
p_\theta\!\left(y^{(k-1)}\mid y^{(k)},c\right)
=\\[-0.4em]
\prod_{i=1}^{L}
p_\theta\!\left(y_i^{(k-1)}\mid y^{(k)},c\right).
\end{gathered}
$$

Here, $k$ is the current refinement round, $y^{(k)}$ is the whole current
sequence, and $y^{(0)}$ is the final output. Positions are parallel within a
round, but round $k-1$ waits for round $k$. The model may revise masks, tokens,
or sequence length depending on the algorithm.

| Design | Dependent decode rounds | Work inside one round | Length mechanism |
|---|---:|---|---|
| causal autoregression | $L$ | one new position with cached prefix | stop token |
| one-shot NAR | $1$ | all $L$ positions | predicted or latent length |
| iterative refinement | $K$ | usually many or all positions | fixed, predicted, inserted, or collapsed |
| block diffusion | $K\lceil L/B\rceil$ | one block of at most $B$ positions | append blocks until stopping |

In the last row, $B$ is block size and $K$ is the number of denoising rounds per
block. This table counts dependency, not FLOPs or wall-clock time.

## Why an independent draft can mix valid translations

Translation is multimodal: one source sentence can have several valid targets.
If one mode says “I do not know” and another says “I don't know,” independent
position predictions can combine pieces of both. The resulting per-position
distributions, the token marginals, may each look plausible while the joint
sentence does not. Repetition and omission are the visible symptoms. Their cause
is the conditional independence assumption, so models that restore some
dependence between positions can reduce them.

Early systems reduced this uncertainty in two ways. Gu et al. used a fertility
latent, an integer count describing how many target positions each source token
produces. It supplies an alignment and helps determine output length. They also
trained on decoded outputs from an autoregressive teacher. Sequence-level
knowledge distillation, which trains a student model on a teacher model's
outputs, replaces each set of human references with a narrower
teacher-generated target [@kim2016seqkd]. Zhou et al. measured this effect as
lower alignment-based word-translation entropy on WMT14 English-German. In
their experiments, stronger non-autoregressive students tended to benefit from
more complex distilled data [@zhou2020understandingkd]. This is an empirical
proxy and capacity trend, not a general theorem about the true sequence entropy.

Distillation was central to classic non-autoregressive translation, but it is
not a mathematical requirement for all parallel generation. It changes the
training distribution, transfers the teacher's errors and preferences, and can
make a student's apparent speed-quality result depend on an unreported teacher.
A fair record names the teacher, decoding method, and whether evaluation uses
human references or teacher outputs.

## Refinement predates diffusion language models

Several pre-diffusion systems added structure without returning to strict
left-to-right decoding:

| Method | Training or decoding move | How it handles length | What remains serial |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mask-Predict | mask low-confidence positions and predict them again | predict length before refinement | a fixed number of refinement rounds |
| Levenshtein Transformer | alternate deletion, placeholder insertion, and token filling | grow and shrink the sequence | edit iterations |
| CTC-based decoding | emit blanks and repeated labels, then collapse a monotonic alignment | marginalize compatible alignments | usually one or a few model rounds |
| Glancing Transformer | reveal selected reference tokens during training | predict length at inference | no iterative inference in its one-pass form |
| SUNDAE | train on unrolled denoising steps and repeatedly repair token sequences | usually fix a canvas | denoising iterations |

Mask-Predict improved over one-shot decoding by spending a predetermined number
of confidence-based refinement rounds [@ghazvininejad2019maskpredict]. The
partially autoregressive Levenshtein Transformer made insertion and deletion
explicit [@gu2019levenshtein]. Connectionist temporal classification (CTC)
systems marginalized, that is, summed probability over, monotonic alignments
containing blanks and repeats [@libovicky2018ctcnat;
@chan2020imputer]. Glancing training exposed a decreasing number of target
tokens as training progressed [@qian2021glat], while SUNDAE trained a denoiser
through more than one of its own predicted states [@savinov2022sundae].

These methods established useful operations: draft, mask, insert, delete,
collapse, and refine. At the algorithmic level, Mask-Predict resembles
absorbing-state diffusion, the mask-based corruption process defined in the next
section, but it was not derived as the reverse chain of D3PM and does
not inherit a diffusion likelihood bound merely because it uses masks.
Comparisons of training objectives should keep the two apart.

## Put diffusion on categorical states

D3PM replaces Gaussian corruption with a Markov chain over a finite vocabulary
[@austin2021d3pm]. Represent one token as a one-hot vector $x_t\in\{0,1\}^{V}$,
where $V$ is vocabulary size. With a column-stochastic transition matrix
$Q_t\in[0,1]^{V\times V}$, whose columns are each a probability distribution
over the next state, one forward step is

$$
\begin{aligned}
q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})
&=\operatorname{Cat}(x_t;Q_t x_{t-1}),\\
\bar Q_t&=Q_tQ_{t-1}\cdots Q_1.
\end{aligned}
$$

and the direct marginal is

$$
q(x_t\mid x_0)
=\operatorname{Cat}(x_t;\bar Q_t x_0).
$$

Here, $q$ is the fixed forward process; $t$ is a corruption step;
$\operatorname{Cat}(x;\pi)$ is a categorical distribution with probability
vector $\pi$; and $\bar Q_t$ is the cumulative transition. For a sequence, the
usual construction corrupts token positions independently even though the
reverse model reads the whole corrupted sequence.

An absorbing process adds a special mask state $m$ that a token can enter but
never leave. In continuous time, the single-position marginal can be written

$$
\begin{gathered}
q(z_t\mid x)=\operatorname{Cat}(z_t;\pi_t(x)),\\
\pi_t(x)=\alpha_t x+(1-\alpha_t)m,\\
t\in[0,1].
\end{gathered}
$$

Here, $x$ is the clean one-hot token, $z_t$ is its corrupted state,
$m$ is the one-hot mask token, $\pi_t(x)$ is the displayed categorical
probability vector, and $\alpha_t$ is a decreasing keep probability with ideal
endpoints $\alpha_0=1$ and $\alpha_1=0$. Because a masked token stays masked
for the rest of the forward process, the network receives sequences made from
clean vocabulary items and a known mask symbol, rather than arbitrary Gaussian
vectors that later need rounding.

Continuous embedding diffusion is a different branch. Diffusion-LM corrupts
word embeddings and uses gradients through the continuous state for controllable
generation [@li2022diffusionlm]. Plaid develops a likelihood-based continuous
language model at larger scale [@gulrajani2023plaid]. Those models must connect
continuous outputs back to discrete tokens; absorbing diffusion stays categorical
throughout. Results from the two branches should not be merged into one quality
claim.

## Derive the masked-diffusion training loss

For the absorbing process, a substitution-based reverse parameterization copies
unmasked tokens and predicts a clean-token distribution only at masked positions.
Under that parameterization, the continuous-time negative evidence lower bound,
a tractable upper bound on the negative log-likelihood of the data, reduces to
[@sahoo2024mdlm; @shi2024md4]

$$
\begin{gathered}
\ell_\theta(x,z_t)
=\sum_{i:\,z_t^{(i)}=m}\\[-0.3em]
\quad\times\left[-\log p_\theta\!\left(x^{(i)}\mid z_t,t\right)\right],\\
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{MDLM}}
=\int_0^1
\frac{-\alpha_t'}{1-\alpha_t}
\\[-0.3em]
\quad\times\mathbb E_{x,z_t}\!\left[\ell_\theta(x,z_t)\right]dt.
\end{gathered}
$$

Here, $x=(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(L)})$ is a clean sequence; $z_t$ is produced by
independently masking its positions with keep probability $\alpha_t$;
$\alpha_t'=d\alpha_t/dt$; $i$ indexes positions currently equal to mask $m$;
and $\ell_\theta$ sums negative log-probabilities over those positions, using
$p_\theta(x^{(i)}\mid z_t,t)$ as the model's clean-token probability at position
$i$. Because $\alpha_t$ decreases, the weight
$-\alpha_t'/(1-\alpha_t)$ is nonnegative. In practice, training samples times
and masking patterns rather than evaluating the integral exactly. The apparent
singularity at the clean endpoint is interpreted as a limit; the probability of
observing a masked position vanishes there, and implementations use numerically
stable finite sampling.

The inner term is masked-token cross-entropy. The diffusion objective is
therefore a weighted family of masked-language-model losses over many corruption
levels. It differs from ordinary BERT training, which teaches a bidirectional
encoder to fill in masked tokens: BERT uses a particular masking recipe and was
not defined with this reverse process, carry-over rule, time weighting, or
likelihood bound. An existing masked language model does not become a complete
generator until its training and sampling procedures supply those missing
pieces.

Generation starts from an output canvas, a fixed-length sequence of $L$ masks.
At each reverse step, the model predicts clean tokens from the entire current
state, the sampler reveals a schedule-dependent subset, and the absorbing
reverse parameterization carries already revealed tokens forward. This
procedure, which draws each state from the learned reverse chain in order, is
called ancestral sampling. Unlike confidence-based Mask-Predict variants, the
ancestral sampler need not re-mask a revealed token. The final step must remove
every remaining mask. Length $L$ still has to be chosen, predicted, or handled
by a blockwise extension.

## Distinguish concrete-score caching from a KV cache

SEDD describes a continuous-time discrete diffusion through ratios of noisy
marginal probabilities. For neighboring sequences $x$ and $y$ that differ at
one token position, its concrete score is

$$
s_t(x)_y=\frac{p_t(y)}{p_t(x)}.
$$

Here, $p_t$ is the noisy sequence distribution at time $t$, and $s_t(x)_y$ is
the ratio associated with the transition from $x$ to $y$. A neural network
approximates the ratios required by the sparse token transition graph rather
than representing an exponentially large sequence transition matrix. SEDD's
score-entropy objective improved perplexity, a likelihood-based measure on
which lower is better, over earlier diffusion language models and was
competitive with GPT-2-scale autoregressive baselines in its experiments
[@lou2023sedd]. Its reported network-evaluation tradeoff is internal
to those tested samplers; one full-sequence diffusion evaluation is not cost
equivalent to one cached autoregressive token step.

RADD specializes the score for absorbing diffusion. It factorizes the required
ratio into a clean-data conditional distribution and a known time-dependent
scalar [@ou2024radd]. If $x_t^{i\leftarrow y}$ replaces mask position $i$ in
$x_t$ with clean token $y$, then the relation for the true (population)
distribution is

$$
\begin{gathered}
\frac{p_t\!\left(x_t^{i\leftarrow y}\right)}{p_t(x_t)}
=\frac{\alpha_t}{1-\alpha_t}\\[-0.2em]
\quad\times
p_0\!\left(X_i=y\mid X_U=x_{t,U}\right).
\end{gathered}
$$

Here, $U$ is the set of unmasked positions; $X_U=x_{t,U}$ means that the clean
random sequence $X$ agrees with the visible tokens in $x_t$; $p_0$ is the clean
data distribution; and $\alpha_t/(1-\alpha_t)$ is the known schedule factor.
The learned conditional on the right need not take $t$ as input even though the
analytic scalar remains time-dependent. If a reverse transition leaves the
corrupted sequence unchanged, that denoiser's
output can be reused at the next time point. This is model-output caching across
an unchanged state. It is different from a causal KV cache, which reuses prefix
keys and values while appending a new token.

RADD also connects absorbing diffusion to any-order autoregressive
factorizations. The probability model may reveal variables in many orders rather
than one fixed left-to-right order. That representational equivalence does not
make the execution plans equivalent: a bidirectional denoiser can still score a
whole canvas repeatedly.

## Recover length and prefix caching with blocks

Full-sequence masked diffusion normally begins with a fixed canvas. Full
bidirectional attention also changes hidden states throughout that canvas after
each reveal, so the standard causal prefix KV cache cannot simply be carried
between rounds. Block diffusion changes the factorization: it generates blocks
autoregressively, then denoises positions within the current block in parallel
[@arriola2025blockdiffusion]. Completed blocks form a stable prefix, so their KV
state can be cached, and generation can continue for an arbitrary number of
blocks.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-nar-spectrum
//| fig-cap: "Dependency structure: autoregression is serial by token, block diffusion is serial across blocks, and full masked diffusion refines a fixed canvas."
digraph {
  bgcolor="transparent";
  rankdir=TB;
  nodesep=0.3; ranksep=0.45;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10, color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fillcolor="#f1ece1", penwidth=1.1];
  edge [fontsize=9, fontname="Helvetica", color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280"];
  ar [label="Autoregressive\none token per step\ncausal prefix cache"];
  bd [label="Block diffusion\ncausal across blocks\nparallel within a block", color="#3b82f6", penwidth=1.6];
  md [label="Full masked diffusion\nfixed canvas\nparallel refinement rounds"];
  ar -> bd [label="increase block size"];
  bd -> md [label="one full block"];
}
```

The following runnable makes only this dependency accounting concrete. It
assumes that a masked pass predicts every position in its current block, ignores
prompt prefill, and counts position predictions without assigning them a
hardware cost.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
from math import ceil

length = 128
rounds = 8
block_size = 16

autoregressive = {
    "dependent_evaluations": length,
    "position_predictions": length,
}
full_masked = {
    "dependent_evaluations": rounds,
    "position_predictions": length * rounds,
}
block_diffusion = {
    "dependent_evaluations": ceil(length / block_size) * rounds,
    "position_predictions": length * rounds,
}

for name, cost in [
    ("autoregressive", autoregressive),
    ("full masked", full_masked),
    ("block diffusion", block_diffusion),
]:
    print(
        f"{name:16} dependent={cost['dependent_evaluations']:3d}, "
        f"positions={cost['position_predictions']:4d}"
    )
```
::::

With these assumptions, full masked diffusion has the shortest dependency chain
but predicts eight times as many token positions as cached autoregression. Block
diffusion lies between them in dependency depth while doing the same illustrative
number of within-block position predictions as full masked diffusion. Actual
latency depends on attention shape, kernels, batch, memory traffic, and how much
parallel hardware each evaluation can use.

## Read scale demonstrations as scoped evidence

Large diffusion language models established that models with this objective
can be trained or adapted beyond the earlier GPT-2-scale experiments. They did
not create one controlled comparison in which only the factorization changed.

| System | What its construction demonstrates | What it does not establish by itself |
|---|---|---|
| LLaDA 8B | masked diffusion can be pretrained from scratch and instruction-tuned | parity with an externally trained 8B autoregressive model under matched data and compute |
| Dream 7B | autoregressive weights can initialize a diffusion model | the same result from diffusion pretraining alone |
| LLaDA-MoE | a 7B-total, 1.4B-active sparse diffusion model can train on roughly 20T tokens | equal cost or quality to a matched sparse autoregressive run |
| LLaDA 2.0 | converted autoregressive MoE weights can produce diffusion models up to 100B total parameters | a 100B diffusion model trained from scratch |

LLaDA's paper reports strong results against its own autoregressive baselines and
selected external models, including an 8B model trained from scratch
[@nie2025llada]. Dream instead initializes from Qwen2.5 autoregressive weights
[@ye2025dream]. LLaDA-MoE reports 7B total parameters, 1.4B active parameters
(the weights used for each token), and approximately 20T training tokens
[@zhu2025lladamoe]. LLaDA 2.0 converts
pretrained autoregressive models through staged block and full-sequence diffusion
training, reaching 100B total parameters in its sparse variant [@bie2025llada2].
These are distinct claims about training route, active compute, and total model
capacity.

Mercury and Seed Diffusion also report high code-generation throughput
[@khanna2025mercury; @song2025seeddiffusion]. Those results show that engineered
diffusion systems can occupy useful speed-quality operating points. Because the
reports use different models, tokenizers, accelerators, output lengths, batches,
and quality suites, their speedups do not transfer as one multiplier for the
model class.

A release that pairs a diffusion model with an autoregressive model of the same
family removes several of those differences at once. When one lab builds the
diffusion model on the architecture and parameter budget of its own
autoregressive model and reports both on one evaluation suite, model size,
active compute, and benchmarks match. The pairing is still not controlled in
the strict sense. The diffusion model may add components such as a separate
encoder or a new output head, it runs its own sampler, and the lab may not say
whether training started from the autoregressive weights or how much training
each model received. Such a pairing can show two things: the quality cost of
the diffusion design at matched size, task by task, and the serving regime in
which its speed claim holds.

Per-user speed, the tokens per second one request receives, and cost at high
concurrency are separate measurements. At small batch sizes an autoregressive
decode step reads the active weights to produce one token per request, so it
is limited by memory bandwidth and most of the accelerator's arithmetic
capacity sits idle (@sec-serving-problem). A diffusion round applies the
weights it loads to every position of a block, which raises the arithmetic
done per byte read and turns that idle capacity into more tokens for the same
request. At high concurrency, batching many autoregressive requests already
keeps the arithmetic units busy, and the extra positions a diffusion round
scores, which the runnable above counts, become paid work. The per-user gain
can then shrink, and the cost per generated token can exceed autoregression's.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

- Google DeepMind announced the open-weight DiffusionGemma 26B A4B on 10 June
  2026 [@odonoghue2026diffusiongemma]. It is built on the Gemma 4 26B A4B
  mixture-of-experts architecture, with 25.2B total and 3.8B active
  parameters. An autoregressive encoder writes the prompt and each finished
  256-token canvas into the KV cache, and a decoder with bidirectional
  attention over the canvas denoises the next canvas in at most 48 steps. The
  model is therefore a block diffusion design, the last row of the dependency
  table earlier in this chapter [@google2026diffusiongemma]. Neither the model
  card nor the launch post says whether training started from Gemma 4 weights.
- The model card places it below Gemma 4 26B A4B on 14 of its 15 benchmark
  rows. The gap is about five points on knowledge tests and wider on
  reasoning-heavy tasks: MMLU Pro 77.6 versus 82.6 percent, LiveCodeBench v6
  69.1 versus 77.1, GPQA Diamond 73.2 versus 82.3, and AIME 2026 without tools
  69.1 versus 88.3. The exception is Humanity's Last Exam without tools, 11.0
  versus 8.7 percent. The diffusion scores use the card's recommended
  entropy-bounded sampler, and the card does not state Gemma 4's decoding
  settings [@google2026diffusiongemma].
- On speed, the card reports 15 to 20 tokens per forward pass and per-user
  generation above 1,100 tokens per second at low batch sizes on an H100 in
  8-bit floating point (FP8), and the launch post claims up to four times
  faster generation than autoregressive models such as Gemma 4 on dedicated
  GPUs [@google2026diffusiongemma; @odonoghue2026diffusiongemma]. The post
  places the advantage at low-to-medium batch sizes on a single accelerator
  and states that at high request rates the parallel decoding “offers
  diminishing returns and can result in higher serving costs”
  [@odonoghue2026diffusiongemma]. These are Google's own figures, and neither
  page reports the two models' speeds at matched batch sizes. The pairing
  therefore shows a quality cost that is largest on reasoning-heavy tasks and
  a per-user speed gain that its authors confine to low concurrency.
- Inception describes its commercial Mercury 2.5, announced in September 2026,
  as, to its knowledge, the largest diffusion language model ever trained. It
  claims 1,107 tokens per second on “widely-available NVIDIA GPUs,” quality
  comparable to GPT-5.6 Luna (Low), Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, and Claude Haiku
  4.5, and list prices of USD 0.20 and 0.75 per million input and output
  tokens. The announcement names no benchmark, batch size, or hardware count
  and cites no third-party measurement [@inception2026mercury25].
:::

## Benchmark the deployed generator

A reproducible comparison fixes the task and reports every decoding setting
that affects the result:

| Dimension | Report |
|---|---|
| quality | likelihood bound or perplexity with identical tokenization, task metrics, and human evaluation where needed |
| dependency | output length, denoising rounds, block size, and network-function evaluations |
| work | positions scored per evaluation, attention pattern, active parameters, and any skipped or cached states |
| latency | time to first visible output, time to complete, and per-request latency at declared batch |
| throughput | requests and tokens per second, including tokenizer and post-processing policy |
| hardware | accelerator, count, precision, compiler, kernels, and memory limits |
| output policy | fixed or predicted length, stop rule, mask schedule, confidence rule, and sampling randomness |

Perplexity is not directly comparable when tokenizers differ because a “token”
then represents different amounts of text. Tokens per second has the same
problem. Character or byte throughput can supplement it, but quality and latency
must still be measured on the same requests. For interactive use, a system that
finishes quickly but exposes no stable prefix may also feel different from a
streaming autoregressive system with a low time to first token.

Method choice follows the workload:

| Workload | Useful starting point | Main risk to test |
|---|---|---|
| open-ended streaming chat | autoregressive or blockwise generation | end-to-end latency and stop behavior |
| fixed-length infilling or constrained editing | masked diffusion or iterative refinement | mask schedule and global consistency |
| translation with strict latency target | one-shot or iterative NAR | mode mixing, length, and teacher dependence |
| batch code completion | benchmark AR, block, and full diffusion under one harness | tokenizer-adjusted throughput and correctness |
| arbitrary-order completion | masked or any-order model | calibration under unusual reveal orders |

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested

It remains unsettled where diffusion language models beat autoregression after
quality, hardware, output length, and serving software are controlled. Parallel
position updates and bidirectional context are advantages for fixed-canvas
editing and arbitrary-order completion. Autoregression retains a simple stop
rule, stable streaming prefix, and mature causal caching. Scale demonstrations
remove “these models cannot be made large” as a blanket objection, but parameter
count and author-reported throughput do not prove frontier-quality or
cost-matched parity. Same-family pairings narrow the question to two
measurements: the quality the diffusion design gives up at matched size, and
whether its per-user speed at low concurrency carries over to the batch sizes
of shared serving. The current evidence establishes more viable designs for
text generation and leaves open whether any of them will replace autoregression.
Diffusion can also work inside autoregressive decoding, as a small block
diffusion drafter whose proposals the autoregressive target verifies, which
leaves the target's output distribution unchanged (@sec-faster-decoding)
[@chen2026dflash].
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Lower-layer constraint

The serving stack determines whether parallel token prediction becomes a
latency win. A full masked round exposes parallel work but often recomputes a
bidirectional canvas. Autoregression exposes little parallelism within one
request but reuses a causal prefix. Block diffusion trades between those
properties. The decisive measurements are network evaluations, positions
recomputed, cache bytes, memory bandwidth, batch, and kernels. A round count
such as “eight rounds” describes the algorithm; its latency has to be measured
on the serving stack.
:::
